title: Quasiparticle Diffusion for the Toda Fluid in Equilibrium
authors: Seema Chahal, Alberto Brollo, Indranil Mukherjee, Abhishek Dhar, Anupam Kundu, Herbert Spohn
abstract: Many-body integrable systems can be understood as a gas of quasiparticles. They propagate ballistically and drive large-scale transport. However, with the exception of the hard rods system, no tools have been available to numerically track such quasiparticles. Focusing on the Toda fluid, whose integrability relies on the availability of a Lax pair, we present a numerical scheme to track quasiparticle trajectories as determined by the time-dependent eigenvectors of the Lax matrix. Simulating the Toda fluid in thermal equilibrium, this tracking scheme is used to numerical confirm Brownian motion of a quasiparticle. Simulated is also the motion of a tagged particle. Our numerical results for the diffusion constant matches with a novel TBA prediction. We believe our numerical scheme can be extended to other classical many-particle models possessing a Lax matrix.
summary: The paper develops a novel numerical technique using the eigenvectors of the Lax matrix to track quasiparticle motion in the integrable Toda fluid at equilibrium. By simulating this process and comparing results against advanced theoretical tools like TBA, the authors confirm Brownian diffusion for quasiparticles and derive quantitative predictions for transport coefficients like the diffusion constant.
main_problem: To numerically track quasiparticle diffusion for the Toda fluid in thermal equilibrium and extend these tracking methods to other integrable systems possessing a Lax matrix.
main_result: The numerical simulations confirm Brownian motion for both individual quasiparticles and tagged particles, with calculated diffusion constants matching novel predictions from Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz (TBA) theory.
method: The authors developed a specialized numerical scheme based on tracking the time-dependent eigenvectors of the Lax matrix associated with the integrable Toda fluid Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The system is the classical Toda fluid, defined by an exponential interaction potential. Its dynamics are governed by conserved quantities derived from the compatibility condition involving a Lax matrix, placing it within the framework of completely integrable systems studied via Generalized Gibbs Ensembles (GGE).
key_observables: Diffusion constant ($D(w)$), average quasiparticle velocity ($\langle v_\alpha angle_{P,V}$), and the velocity autocorrelation function $\langle v_\alpha(t)v_\alpha(0)angle$.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$) or inverse temperature ($ eta$), Pressure ($P$), and system size ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that quasiparticle motion can be accurately tracked via eigenvectors of the Lax matrix, which is mathematically sound but noted to break down visually at high densities.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate sample particle trajectories (Fig 1), eigenvector evolution (Fig 2), and crucially compare numerical results for $	ext{veff}(w)$ and $D(w)$ against analytical TBA predictions (Figs 6, 7).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the Lax pair formalism and conserved quantities to deriving macroscopic properties using GGE/TBA. It then presents the core numerical method for tracking quasiparticles, culminating in comparisons of diffusion constants derived both numerically and theoretically.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, generalizable methodology (eigenvector tracking) to study transport coefficients like diffusion in complex integrable many-body systems, bridging spectral theory with non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The plots show one sample of Toda particle trajectories. The tem- perature of the Toda fluid is 1 and density is 0.25 in (a) and 1.65 in (b). For better visibility, these panels are zoomed-in views of trajectories from 100 Toda particles.

Figure 2: Panels (a) and (b) display the evolution of a representative eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λα = 0.9976. In panel (a), the probability density in index space resulting from the eigenvector is shown at selected time instants. The motion of the peaks is clearly visible and their projection onto the index–time plane is indicated by the light blue line. Panel (b) presents the corresponding heatmap, highlighting the left-to-right propagation of the eigenvector together with its small spatial width.

Figure 3: Comparing representative quasiparticle trajectories: the argmax rule (black broken line), having jumps indicated by black dashed segments, and the |ψ|2 rule of Eq. (32), yielding a smooth trajectory (red solid line). The quasipar- ticle is labeled by the eigenvalue λα = 0.9976. The light blue lines display the underlying Toda particle trajectories.

Figure 4: Schematically illustrating the contribution of initial-state noise to dif- fusion. A tagged quasiparticle, initially at the origin (red line), moves with an effective velocity veff(w) through a noisy, homogeneous background. Quasipar- ticles from each mesoscopic fluid cell propagate with distinct effective velocities and fluctuating particle numbers. These density fluctuations propagate ballisti- cally and scatter with the tagged quasiparticle. Over a time interval ¯t, the tagged quasiparticle trajectory is influenced by quasiparticles of rapidity w′ that origi- nated within a spatial region of extent ℓ= |veff(w) −veff(w′)|¯t.

Figure 5: Plots comparing the simulation (blue circles) and analytical results given by Eq. (20) (red dashed line) for the density of states across three set of parameters: (a) P = 0.32, β = 0.5, yielding an average stretch per particle ν = 2.58, (b) P = 1, β = 1, with ν = 0.58, and (c) P = 1.4, β = 1, with ν = 0.06. For all three plots, N = 500, ∆= 0.05, and averages have been taken over R = 105 samples. The density of the Toda fluid is increasing from left to right.
